abase.definition: to humiliate or degrade, especially oneself
abase.sentence: He abased himself before the committee, apologizing so profusely that even his critics grew uncomfortable.

abash.definition: to embarrass or unsettle someone's composure
abash.sentence: Nothing abashed her: heckling, hostile questions, and open laughter left her delivery entirely unshaken.

abate.definition: to lessen in intensity or degree
abate.sentence: Only when the storm abated did the crew venture onto the deck to assess the damage.

abdicate.definition: to formally give up power or responsibility
abdicate.sentence: By refusing to investigate the fraud, the board effectively abdicated its duty to shareholders.

aberrant.definition: departing sharply from what is normal or expected
aberrant.sentence: A single aberrant reading did not trouble her; it was the pattern of anomalies that demanded explanation.

aberration.definition: a departure from what is normal or expected
aberration.sentence: The senator dismissed his outburst as an aberration, though colleagues recalled several similar episodes.

abet.definition: to help or encourage, usually in wrongdoing
abet.sentence: The clerk who forged the signatures was convicted, as was the manager who abetted him.

abeyance.definition: a state of temporary suspension or inactivity
abeyance.sentence: The lawsuit was held in abeyance while both parties pursued a private settlement.

abhor.definition: to regard with disgust and hatred
abhor.sentence: She abhorred flattery, and courtiers who praised her extravagantly found themselves quickly out of favor.

abide.definition: to tolerate; to endure or remain
abide.sentence: He could abide criticism of his methods but not of the motives behind them.

abject.sentence: The report described abject poverty that decades of aid had somehow failed to relieve.

abjure.definition: to renounce formally, especially under oath
abjure.sentence: Forced to abjure his findings publicly, the astronomer nonetheless kept circulating them among colleagues.

abound.definition: to exist in great numbers or quantity
abound.sentence: Rumors abounded after the merger, though executives insisted nothing had been decided.

aboveboard.sentence: The auditors found the transaction entirely aboveboard, however unusual its timing appeared.

abrasive.sentence: His abrasive style alienated allies who agreed with nearly every position he took.

abreast.definition: up to date with current information
abreast.sentence: Keeping abreast of the literature consumed the hours she had hoped to spend on experiments.

abridge.definition: to shorten while keeping the essentials
abridge.sentence: The editor abridged the memoir severely, cutting three hundred pages without losing the argument.

abrogate.sentence: The new government abrogated the treaty within weeks, citing terms it called unenforceable.

abscission.definition: the act of cutting off; natural shedding of leaves
abscission.sentence: Abscission of the leaves follows a chemical signal, not merely the arrival of cold weather.

abscond.definition: to leave secretly, especially to avoid capture
abscond.sentence: The treasurer absconded with the endowment, and auditors traced the funds through four countries.

abstain.definition: to refrain deliberately from doing something
abstain.sentence: Two members voted against the measure and a third abstained, citing a conflict of interest.

abstemious.definition: sparing, especially in eating and drinking
abstemious.sentence: Abstemious by habit, he ate lightly at banquets that left other guests immobile.

abstruse.sentence: Her argument was sound but so abstruse that only specialists could follow its middle section.

abut.sentence: The new development abuts protected wetlands, which is why the permit drew such scrutiny.

abysmal.sentence: Attendance was abysmal, and the theater closed before the season ended.

abyss.definition: a deep or seemingly bottomless chasm
abyss.sentence: Between his stated principles and his conduct lay an abyss no rhetoric could bridge.

accede.definition: to agree or yield to a demand
accede.sentence: The administration acceded to the students' demands only after a month of daily protests.

accentuate.definition: to emphasize or make more noticeable
accentuate.sentence: The stark lighting accentuated flaws the painter had spent months trying to conceal.

access.definition: the right or means of approaching something
access.sentence: Access to the archive was granted grudgingly, and only for a single afternoon.

accessible.sentence: She wrote an accessible account of quantum theory without diluting a single essential idea.

acclaim.sentence: The novel met with critical acclaim abroad long before publishers at home would touch it.

accolade.definition: an award or expression of praise
accolade.sentence: The prize was the highest accolade in her field, and she received it at thirty-one.

accord.sentence: The two delegations reached an accord on trade but remained divided over fishing rights.

accretion.definition: gradual growth by addition or accumulation
accretion.sentence: The doctrine developed by accretion, each generation of judges adding a qualification.

acerbic.sentence: His acerbic reviews were feared by playwrights and quoted with delight by everyone else.

acidulous.definition: somewhat sour in taste or manner
acidulous.sentence: She offered an acidulous compliment that left the honoree unsure whether to thank her.

acme.sentence: The cathedral is often called the acme of a style that took two centuries to mature.

acolyte.sentence: The economist was trailed by acolytes who repeated his phrases more faithfully than his reasoning.

acquiesce.definition: to accept or comply reluctantly, without protest
acquiesce.sentence: She acquiesced to the schedule change, though her silence was plainly not approval.

acquisitive.definition: eager to acquire possessions or wealth
acquisitive.sentence: An acquisitive collector, he bought whole libraries merely to secure a few manuscripts.

acrid.definition: sharply bitter in smell, taste, or tone
acrid.sentence: Acrid smoke drifted through the corridors hours after the fire had been put out.

acrimonious.sentence: The negotiations grew so acrimonious that mediators separated the parties into different buildings.

acrimony.sentence: Decades of acrimony between the families ended, improbably, over a shared legal problem.

activism.definition: vigorous action to bring about political or social change
activism.sentence: Her activism began with a local zoning fight and ended in the national legislature.

actuate.definition: to set in motion; to motivate
actuate.sentence: What actuated the reform was not principle but the threat of losing federal funding.

acumen.sentence: Her political acumen let her count votes weeks before the whips could.

adage.definition: a traditional saying expressing common wisdom
adage.sentence: He answered every objection with an adage, which passed for wisdom until someone examined it.

adamant.sentence: She was adamant that the data be released in full, whatever the political cost.

adept.sentence: Adept at reading a room, he abandoned his prepared remarks after the first minute.

adequate.sentence: The funding was adequate to keep the clinic open, not to expand the services it offered.

adhere.definition: to stick fast; to follow closely
adhere.sentence: Researchers who adhere rigidly to the protocol sometimes miss what the anomalies are telling them.

adherent.definition: a supporter of a cause or person
adherent.sentence: The movement attracted adherents faster than it could articulate what it actually wanted.

adjudicate.definition: to judge or settle a dispute formally
adjudicate.sentence: The panel was asked to adjudicate a claim that neither side could document convincingly.

adjure.sentence: The letter adjured him to withdraw before the vote, invoking loyalties two decades old.

admonish.sentence: The judge admonished counsel for the remark but declined to declare a mistrial.

admonitory.sentence: His admonitory tone made the advice sound like a verdict already delivered.

adroit.definition: clever and skillful, especially in handling situations
adroit.sentence: An adroit negotiator, she conceded the small points loudly and the crucial ones never.

adulation.sentence: The adulation of his early admirers did more damage to his prose than any critic could.

adulterate.definition: to make impure by adding inferior substances
adulterate.sentence: Merchants adulterated the spice with ground husks, a fraud detectable only under magnification.

adumbrate.sentence: The preface adumbrates an argument the book itself never quite develops.

adventitious.sentence: The resemblance is adventitious, arising from convergent pressures rather than shared ancestry.

adverse.sentence: The drug was withdrawn after adverse effects appeared in a small fraction of patients.

adversity.sentence: Her reputation rests less on her triumphs than on her composure in adversity.

advert.definition: to refer to something in speech or writing
advert.sentence: He adverted briefly to the scandal, then returned to the budget as though nothing had happened.

advocate.sentence: She advocated a gradual transition, warning that abrupt reform would collapse under its own costs.

aerie.definition: a lofty nest or dwelling high above
aerie.sentence: From his aerie on the top floor, the editor rarely saw the reporters he directed.

aesthete.definition: one devoted to beauty and art
aesthete.sentence: An aesthete to the end, he chose his furniture more carefully than his friends.

aesthetic.definition: concerned with beauty or artistic taste
aesthetic.sentence: The objection was aesthetic rather than practical: the bridge worked, but nobody could bear looking at it.

affable.definition: friendly and easy to talk to
affable.sentence: His affable manner concealed a bargaining style that gave away almost nothing.

affect.definition: to put on a pretense of; to influence
affect.sentence: He affected an indifference to the prize that nobody who knew him believed.

affectation.sentence: The accent was pure affectation, acquired at university and abandoned whenever he was tired.

affected.sentence: Her affected modesty irritated colleagues who had watched her campaign openly for the appointment.

affinity.definition: a natural attraction or close resemblance
affinity.sentence: He felt an affinity for the older painters, whose difficulties resembled his own.

afflict.sentence: The drought afflicted the northern provinces most severely, though the capital drew the coverage.

affluent.sentence: The policy benefited affluent districts that had lobbied for it and few others.

afford.sentence: The vantage point affords a view of the whole valley, which is why the fort was built there.

affront.sentence: The omission of her name was taken as an affront, and she declined to attend.

aggrandize.definition: to increase power, wealth, or importance
aggrandize.sentence: Each reorganization aggrandized the department that proposed it, a pattern nobody named aloud.

aggravate.sentence: The tariff aggravated a shortage that the government had spent a year trying to relieve.

aggregate.definition: a total formed by combining separate parts
aggregate.sentence: In aggregate the reforms saved money, though several districts paid substantially more.

aggrieve.definition: to treat unjustly; to cause grief to
aggrieve.sentence: Aggrieved shareholders sued, arguing the board had concealed the losses for two quarters.

aghast.sentence: Aghast at the proposal, the trustees adjourned without taking a vote.

agitate.definition: to stir up feeling; to campaign vigorously
agitate.sentence: For a decade she agitated for the reform that her successors would take credit for passing.

aide.definition: an assistant to an important person
aide.sentence: An aide leaked the memo, and the minister's denials collapsed within a day.

alacrity.sentence: She accepted the assignment with an alacrity that surprised colleagues expecting resistance.

alchemy.definition: a seemingly magical process of transformation
alchemy.sentence: By some alchemy of editing, a shapeless draft became the year's most admired essay.

alcove.definition: a small recessed space in a room
alcove.sentence: He worked in an alcove off the main hall, hidden from anyone who might interrupt.

alienate.sentence: The tone of the announcement alienated the very donors it had been written to reassure.

allay.definition: to calm or reduce fear or doubt
allay.sentence: Nothing in the statement allayed the concerns of parents who had read the inspection report.

allege.sentence: The complaint alleges misconduct spanning four years, none of it yet corroborated.

alleviate.sentence: The grant alleviated the immediate crisis without addressing why it kept recurring.

allusion.sentence: The speech was thick with allusions to a scandal the speaker never mentioned by name.

allusive.sentence: Her allusive style rewards rereading and frustrates anyone hoping for a plain statement.

aloof.sentence: He remained aloof from factional quarrels, which made him acceptable to both sides.

altruism.sentence: Economists have long puzzled over altruism toward strangers who can never reciprocate.

altruistic.sentence: The gesture was less altruistic than it appeared, as the donor's name went on the building.

amalgam.definition: a mixture or blend of different things
amalgam.sentence: The style is an amalgam of local craft traditions and imported industrial technique.

amalgamate.definition: to combine into a single whole
amalgamate.sentence: The two societies amalgamated in 1908, though their journals stayed separate for decades.

amalgamation.definition: the process of combining into one
amalgamation.sentence: The amalgamation of the archives simplified access and destroyed some useful distinctions.

ambience.definition: the atmosphere or character of a place
ambience.sentence: The restaurant traded on its ambience, since the food itself was unremarkable.

ambiguous.definition: open to more than one interpretation
ambiguous.sentence: The wording was deliberately ambiguous, letting both delegations claim victory at home.

ambivalence.definition: the state of having conflicting feelings
ambivalence.sentence: Her ambivalence about the promotion showed in the three weeks she took to answer.

ambivalent.sentence: Critics were ambivalent: they admired the ambition and distrusted nearly every result.

ambrosia.definition: something delicious; food of the gods
ambrosia.sentence: After a week of rations, the plain bread tasted like ambrosia to the survey team.

ameliorate.definition: to make a bad situation better
ameliorate.sentence: The subsidy ameliorated conditions in the short term without changing what caused them.

amenable.definition: willing to agree or be persuaded
amenable.sentence: He proved amenable to compromise once the deadline made delay more costly than concession.

amend.definition: to change or improve a text or law
amend.sentence: The clause was amended twice before anyone noticed it now contradicted the preamble.

amiable.sentence: An amiable colleague, he was nonetheless ruthless about deadlines he had not set.

amicable.sentence: The dispute ended in an amicable settlement that neither party would discuss publicly.

amorous.sentence: The letters are amorous in tone yet oddly formal, as though written for an audience.

amorphous.sentence: The movement remained amorphous, with no leaders, no platform, and remarkable staying power.

amortize.definition: to pay off a debt gradually
amortize.sentence: The loan is amortized over thirty years, which conceals how much interest it carries.

amply.sentence: The evidence amply supports the narrower claim and says nothing about the broader one.

amuck.sentence: Left unsupervised, the process runs amuck and produces results nobody can reconstruct.

amulet.definition: a charm worn to ward off evil
amulet.sentence: The amulet was buried with its owner, suggesting protection was expected to continue after death.

anachronism.definition: something out of its proper historical time
anachronism.sentence: The wristwatch in the battle scene is an anachronism that reviewers noticed immediately.

anachronistic.definition: belonging to the wrong time period
anachronistic.sentence: His anachronistic courtesies charmed some colleagues and struck others as a performance.

analgesia.definition: the absence or relief of pain
analgesia.sentence: The compound produced analgesia without the sedation that limited earlier treatments.

analgesic.sentence: The analgesic dulled the pain enough for her to work, though not to sleep.

analogous.definition: similar in a way that permits comparison
analogous.sentence: The situation is analogous to the earlier crisis, but the differences matter more than the parallels.

anarchy.sentence: What followed the collapse was not anarchy but a patchwork of local authorities.

anathema.definition: something intensely detested; a formal curse
anathema.sentence: Compromise was anathema to the faction that had built its identity on refusing it.

ancillary.sentence: The ancillary services cost more than the treatment they were meant to support.

androgynous.definition: having both male and female characteristics
androgynous.sentence: The sculpture's androgynous features have frustrated attempts to identify the figure.

anemic.sentence: Growth was anemic for three straight quarters despite the incentives announced with such confidence.

anesthetic.definition: a substance that produces loss of sensation
anesthetic.sentence: The anesthetic wore off sooner than expected, and the procedure had to be paused.

animosity.sentence: Personal animosity, not policy, kept the two committees from meeting for a year.

animus.definition: hostility or ill will motivating action
animus.sentence: The court found no evidence of animus, only administrative carelessness of an impressive scale.

annul.sentence: The election was annulled after observers documented irregularities at a third of the polling stations.

anodyne.sentence: The statement was so anodyne that both factions quoted it approvingly the same afternoon.

anoint.sentence: The retiring chairman anointed a successor, and the board discovered it had no real say.

anomalous.sentence: The anomalous result was reproduced twice before anyone dared publish it.

anomaly.definition: something that deviates from the norm
anomaly.sentence: The anomaly persisted across instruments, which is precisely why it could not be dismissed.

antagonize.sentence: He antagonized the only committee whose support his proposal actually required.

antecedent.sentence: The reform had antecedents in a proposal rejected forty years earlier for the same reasons.

antedate.sentence: The manuscript antedates the invention it describes, which is why scholars suspect a forgery.

antedated.definition: came before in time; dated earlier than actual
antedated.sentence: The contract was antedated by two months, a detail the auditors found immediately.

anthology.sentence: The anthology preserved a dozen poets whose individual volumes had long gone out of print.

anthropocentrism.definition: regarding humans as the central concern
anthropocentrism.sentence: Her critique targets the anthropocentrism implicit in valuing forests only for what they yield us.

anthropomorphic.definition: attributing human traits to nonhuman things
anthropomorphic.sentence: Anthropomorphic descriptions make the behavior vivid and quietly smuggle in assumptions about motive.

antic.sentence: The antics that delighted audiences early on wore thin by the third season.

antipathy.sentence: His antipathy toward the press predated any particular story they had run about him.

antiquated.definition: outdated; belonging to an earlier era
antiquated.sentence: The antiquated filing system survived because replacing it would expose how little had been recorded.

antithesis.sentence: Her patient, evidence-first method was the antithesis of his taste for bold conjecture.

antithetical.sentence: Secrecy of that kind is antithetical to the transparency the charter demands.

apathetic.sentence: Voters were not hostile so much as apathetic, having heard the same promises three elections running.

apathy.sentence: The campaign's real opponent was apathy, not the rival party's thin platform.

apex.sentence: The company reached its apex just before the technology it depended on became obsolete.

aphorism.definition: a short saying expressing a general truth
aphorism.sentence: He wrote in aphorisms, which made him quotable and occasionally unintelligible.

aphoristic.sentence: Her aphoristic prose compresses arguments that other writers would spend chapters unfolding.

aplomb.sentence: She handled the hostile questioning with an aplomb that unnerved her interrogators.

apocryphal.sentence: The story about the burnt manuscript is apocryphal, though biographers repeat it fondly.

apogee.definition: the highest or most distant point
apogee.sentence: The movement reached its apogee in 1968 and fragmented within three years.

apologist.definition: one who defends a doctrine or practice
apologist.sentence: He became an apologist for a policy he had privately called indefensible.

apostate.definition: one who abandons a belief or allegiance
apostate.sentence: Denounced as an apostate, she pointed out that the doctrine itself had changed, not her.

apostle.definition: an ardent early advocate of a cause
apostle.sentence: He was an apostle of open data long before institutions found the idea respectable.

apothegm.sentence: The lecture ended with an apothegm students copied down without quite understanding.

apotheosis.definition: the highest example; elevation to divine status
apotheosis.sentence: The chapel is the apotheosis of a style that elsewhere looks merely ornate.

apparent.definition: clearly visible; seeming rather than actual
apparent.sentence: The apparent contradiction dissolves once you notice the two studies measured different populations.

appease.definition: to pacify by giving in to demands
appease.sentence: Concessions meant to appease the faction only convinced it that more could be extracted.

append.sentence: She appended a dissent that eventually proved more influential than the majority opinion.

appoint.definition: to assign to a position or office
appoint.sentence: He was appointed to the panel after two better-qualified candidates declined.

apposite.sentence: Her example was apposite, cutting off an objection before anyone could raise it.

appreciable.definition: large enough to be noticed or measured
appreciable.sentence: There was no appreciable difference between the groups, though the press release implied otherwise.

apprehension.sentence: She approached the review with apprehension that the first ten minutes entirely dispelled.

apprise.sentence: Nobody apprised the committee of the change until after the contracts were signed.

approach.definition: a way of dealing with something
approach.sentence: Their approach was empirical where his was theoretical, and the two rarely spoke.

approbation.sentence: He craved the approbation of colleagues whose work he had spent years dismissing.

approbatory.sentence: An approbatory nod from the chair was the closest thing to praise the department offered.

appropriate.definition: to take for one's own use, often without permission
appropriate.sentence: The ministry appropriated funds earmarked for schools and reported the shift only years later.

appurtenance.definition: an accessory or minor accompanying item
appurtenance.sentence: The title came with appurtenances of office that cost more to maintain than the salary covered.

appurtenant.definition: belonging to as a subordinate part
appurtenant.sentence: The easement is appurtenant to the land and passes automatically to the next owner.

apropos.sentence: Her question was apropos, though it derailed a presentation the speaker had rehearsed for weeks.

apt.sentence: The metaphor is apt: the institution really does resemble a machine nobody remembers designing.

aquiline.sentence: The portrait exaggerates his aquiline profile, which contemporaries described as unremarkable.

arbiter.definition: one with power to settle disputes
arbiter.sentence: For thirty years the journal was the arbiter of what counted as serious work in the field.

arbitrary.definition: based on whim rather than reason
arbitrary.sentence: The cutoff was arbitrary, and students a single point below it were treated entirely differently.

arbitrate.definition: to settle a dispute as a neutral party
arbitrate.sentence: She was asked to arbitrate a quarrel that both sides preferred to keep alive.

arcane.sentence: The rules were arcane enough that compliance depended on a handful of long-serving clerks.

arch.sentence: Her arch remarks about the committee's efficiency were funnier than anyone there admitted.

archaic.definition: belonging to an earlier period; outdated
archaic.sentence: The statute's archaic language required a specialist to determine what it actually prohibited.

archetype.definition: an original model or typical example
archetype.sentence: The novel established an archetype that a hundred imitators diluted within a decade.

ardent.sentence: An ardent defender of the program, she nonetheless conceded its costs had been understated.

ardor.sentence: The ardor of his early letters gave way to the caution of a man with something to lose.

arduous.sentence: Cataloguing the collection was arduous work that three previous archivists had abandoned.

aria.definition: an elaborate solo song in an opera
aria.sentence: The aria is technically brutal, which is why so few singers attempt it twice.

armada.definition: a large fleet of ships or vehicles
armada.sentence: An armada of trucks arrived at dawn, and the site was cleared before noon.

arrant.definition: complete; utter, in a negative sense
arrant.sentence: The claim was arrant nonsense, and repeating it confidently did not improve it.

arrest.definition: to stop or check the progress of
arrest.sentence: The treatment arrests the disease's progress without reversing the damage already done.

arresting.sentence: The opening image is arresting enough that few viewers notice how conventional the rest becomes.

arriviste.definition: an ambitious newcomer to wealth or status
arriviste.sentence: The old families treated him as an arriviste long after his fortune exceeded theirs.

arrogate.definition: to claim or seize without right
arrogate.sentence: The agency arrogated to itself powers the legislature had deliberately withheld.

artful.definition: clever, often in a cunning way
artful.sentence: His artful phrasing conceded nothing while sounding, to most listeners, like an apology.

articulate.sentence: She was the most articulate member of a panel that badly needed one.

artifact.definition: an object made by humans; a spurious result
artifact.sentence: The spike proved to be an artifact of the instrument rather than a feature of the sample.

artifice.sentence: The apparent spontaneity was pure artifice, rehearsed over several afternoons.

artless.sentence: Her artless account of the meeting revealed more than the official minutes ever would.

artlessness.definition: sincerity; freedom from deceit or affectation
artlessness.sentence: The memoir's artlessness is its charm and, in places, its most serious limitation.
